--- title: "A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️" subtitle: "MATH 4750 / MSSC 5750 Computational Statistics" format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" highlight-style: arrow code-block-bg: true self-contained: false slide-number: c/t incremental: false width: 1800 height: 1000 margin: 0.05 logo: "logo.png" footer: "[mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27](https://mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27/)" theme: ["simple", "slides.scss"] multiplex: false code-link: true fig-cap-location: bottom fig-align: center transition: none ## fade slide convex concave zoom title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: mu-bg.png data-background-size: stretch data-slide-number: none editor: source execute: freeze: auto echo: true purl: true --- # {visibility="hidden"} \def\bx{\mathbf{x}} \def\by{\mathbf{y}} \def\bz{\mathbf{z}} \def\bu{\mathbf{u}} \def\bv{\mathbf{v}} \def\bw{\mathbf{w}} \def\bX{\mathbf{X}} \def\bY{\mathbf{Y}} \def\bZ{\mathbf{Z}} \def\bU{\mathbf{U}} \def\bV{\mathbf{V}} \def\bW{\mathbf{W}} \def\bI{\mathbf{I}} \def\bH{\mathbf{H}} \def\bS{\mathbf{S}} \def\bD{\mathbf{D}} \def\bbeta{\boldsymbol \beta} \def\btheta{\boldsymbol \theta} \def\bmu{\boldsymbol \mu} \def\bSigma{\boldsymbol \Sigma} \def\bLambda{\boldsymbol \Lambda} \def\beps{\boldsymbol \epsilon} \def\T{\text{T}} \def\E{\mathrm{E}} \def\var{\mathrm{Var}} \def\cov{\mathrm{Cov}} \def\cor{\mathrm{Corr}} \def\se{\mathrm{se}} \def\bias{\mathrm{bias}} \def\mse{\mathrm{MSE}} \def\R{\mathbb{R}} \def\P{\mathrm{P}} \def\iid{\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmin}{arg\,min} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmax}{arg\,max} # A Journey Through Functional Data with R

What is functional data?

Representing functional data: basis expansions (monomial, Fourier, splines)

Smoothing penalties and choosing $\lambda$

Bivariate bases: tensor products

Dimension reduction: SVD, PCA, ICA, and functional PCA

::: notes - Supplementary deck (converted from 2-FDAiR.pdf). Main sources: Ramsay and Silverman (2005) *Functional Data Analysis*; Ramsay, Hooker and Graves (2009) *Functional Data Analysis with R and Matlab*; G. Hooker's short course handout; Huang, Shen and Buja (2008) for FPCA. - Everything is implemented with base R (splines, svd) so the ideas are visible; the fda package (`fda-lab.r`) packages them. - Interactive companion: ::: # What Is Functional Data? ## Functional Data: Repeated Measures of a Smooth Process :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} - Data are measurements of **smooth processes** over a continuum (usually time). - We do not want parametric assumptions about those processes. - Often **multiple** curves of the same process; we describe the **variation** between curves. - Frequently high resolution and low noise. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} *"Functional data is multivariate data with an ordering on the dimensions."* (Müller, 2006) $$ y_{ij} = x_i(t_{ij}) + \epsilon_{ij},\qquad x_i(t)\ \text{smooth}. $$ **Functional data** = the functions $x_i(t)$. ::: :::: Applications: medical monitoring (EEG, ECG, fMRI), biology (growth curves), environmental monitoring (weather, pollution), traffic. ## Canadian Weather Data Average daily temperature and precipitation at 35 Canadian weather stations (classical and much used). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) matplot(day, temp, type = "l", lty = 1, col = adjustcolor("#2E5BBA", .5), xlab = "day", ylab = "deg C", main = "Temperature") lines(day, temp[, "Vancouver"], lwd = 3, col = "red") matplot(day, precip, type = "l", lty = 1, col = adjustcolor("#2E5BBA", .5), xlab = "day", ylab = "mm", main = "Precipitation") lines(day, precip[, "Vancouver"], lwd = 3, col = "red") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Weather in Vancouver and the Challenges ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(day, temp[, "Vancouver"], pch = 20, col = "#2E5BBA", xlab = "Day", ylab = "Temperature (deg C)", main = "Vancouver") plot(day, precip[, "Vancouver"], pch = 1, col = "#2E5BBA", xlab = "Day", ylab = "Precipitation (mm)", main = "Vancouver") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: **Challenges:** estimating functions from noisy discrete observations; numerical representation of infinite-dimensional objects; representing variation in infinite dimensions; relationships between functional objects; $n < p = \infty$ (we need smoothness); measures of variation in estimates. # Representing Functional Data ## From Discrete to Functional Data Two problems, two methods: 1. **Represent** non-parametric continuous-time functions: **basis expansions** $$ x(t) = \sum_{k=1}^K c_k\phi_k(t) = \boldsymbol\Phi(t)\mathbf c,\quad \phi_k \text{ pre-defined}. $$ 2. **Reduce noise** in measurements: **smoothing penalties** $$ \hat{\mathbf c} = \argmin_{\mathbf c}\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i - x(t_i)\big)^2 + \lambda\int[Lx(t)]^2dt, $$ where $Lx$ measures the "roughness" of $x$ (e.g. $Lx = x''$) and $\lambda$ trades fit for smoothness. ## Basis Expansions Are Just Regression From multiple regression $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{1i} + \cdots + \epsilon_i$, or with curvature $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1t_i + \beta_2t_i^2 + \cdots$. For one record, $y_i = x(t_i) + \epsilon_i$ with $x(t) = \boldsymbol\Phi(t)\mathbf c$: $$ \hat{\mathbf c} = (\boldsymbol\Phi^\T\boldsymbol\Phi)^{-1}\boldsymbol\Phi^\T\by,\qquad \hat\by = \bS\by,\ \ \bS = \boldsymbol\Phi(\boldsymbol\Phi^\T\boldsymbol\Phi)^{-1}\boldsymbol\Phi^\T. $$ ## The Monomial Basis and Its Problems $\boldsymbol\Phi(t) = (1, t, t^2, t^3, \dots)$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- temp[, "Vancouver"]; tt <- day / 365 Phi_mono <- outer(tt, 0:7, `^`) kappa(Phi_mono); kappa(cbind(1, poly(tt, 7))) # monomials are badly conditioned (Ch 13) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 160809 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 18.97 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fit_mono <- lm(y ~ poly(tt, 7)) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) matplot(day, Phi_mono[, 2:6], type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, ylab = "basis", main = "Monomial basis") plot(day, y, pch = 20, col = "red", main = "Vancouver: degree 7 polynomial"); lines(day, fitted(fit_mono), lwd = 3, col = "#003366") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - Monomial fits have derivatives that behave badly (the second derivative explodes at the ends), and the basis is nearly collinear. ## The Fourier Basis $$ 1,\ \sin(\omega t),\ \cos(\omega t),\ \sin(2\omega t),\ \cos(2\omega t),\ \dots,\qquad \omega = 2\pi/P. $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fourier_basis <- function(t, K, P = 365) { B <- matrix(1, length(t), 1) for (k in 1:K) B <- cbind(B, sin(2 * pi * k * t / P), cos(2 * pi * k * t / P)) B } Phi_f <- fourier_basis(day, 3) fit_f <- lm.fit(Phi_f, y) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) matplot(day, Phi_f[, 2:5], type = "l", lty = c(1, 2, 1, 2), col = c(2, 4, 2, 4), lwd = 2, ylab = "", main = "Fourier basis (k = 1, 2)") plot(day, y, pch = 20, col = "red", main = "Vancouver: 7 Fourier functions"); lines(day, Phi_f %*% fit_f$coefficients, lwd = 3, col = "#003366") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - Advantages: excellent computational properties (orthogonal on equally spaced points; FFT), natural for **periodic** data. But representations are periodic: a problem if the data are not. ## Spline Bases **Truncated power basis** of degree $d$ with knots $\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_K$: $$ 1, t, \dots, t^d, (t-\kappa_1)_+^d, \dots, (t-\kappa_K)_+^d. $$ Piecewise polynomials, joined smoothly ($d-1$ continuous derivatives) at the knots. **B-splines** span the same space with a well-conditioned, compactly supported basis. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(splines) kn <- seq(0, 365, length = 9)[-c(1, 9)] Phi_b <- bs(day, knots = kn, degree = 3, intercept = TRUE) fit_b <- lm.fit(Phi_b, y) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) matplot(day, Phi_b, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, ylab = "", main = "Cubic B-spline basis"); abline(v = kn, lty = 3) plot(day, y, pch = 20, col = "red", main = "Vancouver: B-spline fit"); lines(day, Phi_b %*% fit_b$coefficients, lwd = 3, col = "#003366") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Smoothing Penalties: Roughness and $\lambda$ Use **many** basis functions, then penalize roughness. With a B-spline basis, Eilers and Marx's **P-splines** replace $\int[x'']^2$ by a difference penalty on the coefficients: $$ \hat{\mathbf c}_\lambda = (\boldsymbol\Phi^\T\boldsymbol\Phi + \lambda\bD^\T\bD)^{-1}\boldsymbol\Phi^\T\by,\qquad \bD = \text{second-difference matrix}. $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} yp <- precip[, "Vancouver"] Phi <- bs(day, df = 40, degree = 3, intercept = TRUE); D <- diff(diag(ncol(Phi)), differences = 2) psmooth <- function(lambda) { S <- Phi %*% solve(crossprod(Phi) + lambda * crossprod(D), t(Phi)); list(fit = S %*% yp, df = sum(diag(S))) } plot(day, yp, col = "gray50", main = "Vancouver precipitation: P-spline smooths", xlab = "day", ylab = "mm") cols <- c("#C0392B", "#003366", "#27AE60") for (k in 1:3) lines(day, psmooth(c(0.1, 100, 1e5)[k])$fit, lwd = 3, col = cols[k]) legend("top", paste("lambda =", c(0.1, 100, 1e5)), col = cols, lwd = 3, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Choosing $\lambda$: Generalized Cross-Validation $$ \text{GCV}(\lambda) = \frac{n\,\text{RSS}(\lambda)}{\big(n - \text{tr}\,\bS_\lambda\big)^2} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lams <- 10^seq(-2, 6, length = 40) gcv <- sapply(lams, function(l) { s <- psmooth(l); 365 * sum((yp - s$fit)^2) / (365 - s$df)^2 }) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(lams, gcv, log = "x", type = "l", lwd = 3, xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "GCV"); abline(v = lams[which.min(gcv)], lty = 2) best <- psmooth(lams[which.min(gcv)]) plot(day, yp, col = "gray50", main = sprintf("GCV choice: df = %.1f", best$df)); lines(day, best$fit, lwd = 3, col = "#003366") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - The same idea as ridge regression (deck 04) with a structured penalty; LOOCV shortcut via the smoother matrix (deck 14). ## Bivariate Case: Tensor Product Bases If $\{\phi_i(x)\}_{i=1}^N$ and $\{\psi_j(y)\}_{j=1}^M$ are bases in each dimension, the $NM$ tensor product functions $\phi_i(x)\psi_j(y)$ form a basis for surfaces: $\bB = \bB_x\otimes\bB_y$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} zv <- volcano; xg <- seq(0, 1, length = nrow(zv)); yg <- seq(0, 1, length = ncol(zv)) Bx <- bs(xg, df = 10, intercept = TRUE); By <- bs(yg, df = 8, intercept = TRUE) B <- kronecker(By, Bx) # (87*61) x (10*8) tensor product design cf <- qr.coef(qr(B), as.vector(zv)); zhat <- matrix(B %*% cf, nrow(zv)) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1)) persp(xg, yg, zv, theta = 130, phi = 30, col = "#FFCC00", border = NA, shade = .5, main = "volcano (5307 values)") persp(xg, yg, zhat, theta = 130, phi = 30, col = "#88A0C8", border = NA, shade = .5, main = "80 tensor B-spline coefficients") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - Irregular domains: bivariate splines on **triangulations** (smoothness conditions across triangle edges). # Dimension Reduction ## Singular Value Decomposition $$ \bX_{n\times m} = \bU\bS\bV^\T,\qquad \bU^\T\bU = \bI,\ \bV^\T\bV = \bI,\ \bS = \text{diag}(s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots). $$ **Truncated SVD:** $\bX_k = \bU_k\bS_k\bV_k^\T$ is the closest rank-$k$ matrix to $\bX$ (Eckart-Young). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sv <- svd(volcano) par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1)) for (k in c(1, 2, 5, 20)) { Xk <- sv$u[, 1:k, drop = FALSE] %*% diag(sv$d[1:k], k) %*% t(sv$v[, 1:k, drop = FALSE]) image(Xk, axes = FALSE, col = terrain.colors(60), main = sprintf("rank %d (%.1f%% energy)", k, 100 * sum(sv$d[1:k]^2) / sum(sv$d^2))) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## PCA, Its Geometry, and the SVD Connection - Find the direction $\bv$ with the greatest variation: $\argmax_{\|\bv\|=1}\bv^\T\bX^\T\bX\bv = \argmax\|\bX\bv\|^2$ (centered $\bX$): the leading eigenvector of $\bX^\T\bX$. - From $\bX = \bU\bS\bV^\T$: $\ \bX^\T\bX = \bV\bS^2\bV^\T$, $\ \bX\bX^\T = \bU\bS^2\bU^\T$, and $\bU = \bX\bV\bS^{-1}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} Xc <- scale(t(temp), scale = FALSE) # 35 stations x 365 days, centered s <- svd(Xc); e <- eigen(crossprod(Xc), symmetric = TRUE) c(max_eigenvalue_diff = max(abs(e$values[1:5] - s$d[1:5]^2)), PC_variance_share = round(s$d[1:3]^2 / sum(s$d^2), 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` max_eigenvalue_diff PC_variance_share1 PC_variance_share2 PC_variance_share3 2.328e-10 8.800e-01 8.500e-02 2.100e-02 ``` ::: ::: ## Functional PCA of Canadian Temperatures Treat each station's curve as one observation; the right singular vectors are the **eigenfunctions** $\xi_k(t)$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) mu <- colMeans(t(temp)) matplot(day, s$v[, 1:3] * -1, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 3, col = c("#003366", "#C0392B", "#27AE60"), ylab = expression(xi[k](t)), main = "First three eigenfunctions") legend("bottom", sprintf("PC%d (%.1f%%)", 1:3, 100 * s$d[1:3]^2 / sum(s$d^2)), col = c("#003366", "#C0392B", "#27AE60"), lwd = 3, bty = "n") plot(day, mu, type = "l", lwd = 3, ylim = c(-35, 25), ylab = "deg C", main = "Mean +/- 2 sd along PC1") lines(day, mu + 2 * s$d[1] / sqrt(34) * s$v[, 1], lty = 2, lwd = 2); lines(day, mu - 2 * s$d[1] / sqrt(34) * s$v[, 1], lty = 3, lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - PC1 is roughly "overall warmth" (more variation in winter); PC2 contrasts winter and summer (continental vs maritime climate). ## Station Scores ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sc <- s$u[, 1:2] %*% diag(s$d[1:2]) par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)) plot(-sc, type = "n", xlab = "PC1 score (warm ->)", ylab = "PC2 score") text(-sc, labels = colnames(temp), cex = .8, col = ifelse(colnames(temp) %in% c("Vancouver", "Victoria", "Pr. Rupert"), "red", "#003366")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/99-fdair/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## FPCA with Smoothing and Missing Data - Raw SVD eigenfunctions are noisy when curves are noisy or sparsely observed. - **Regularized FPCA** (Huang, Shen and Buja, 2008): penalized rank-one approximation $$ \min_{\bu,\bv}\ \|\bX - \bu\bv^\T\|_F^2 + \lambda\,\bu^\T\bu\ \bv^\T\boldsymbol\Omega\bv, $$ solved by alternating ridge-type updates; handles missing entries by fitting only observed cells. - Integrating data transformation, smoothing and missing data: and the course code in `FDAiR/shiny/`. ## Independent Component Analysis (ICA) vs. PCA | | PCA | ICA | |---|---|---| | Model | $\bX = \bU\bS$, $\bU^\T\bU = \bI$ | $\bX = \mathbf A\bS$, $\mathbf A$ invertible | | Removes | correlations | correlations **and** higher-order dependence | | Components | ordered by importance | equally important | | Directions | orthogonal | not orthogonal | - The **cocktail party problem**: unmix several microphone recordings into the original voices (course code: `ICA/audio-demo.R`, `fastICA`). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); tt2 <- seq(0, 10, length = 1000) S <- cbind(sin(2 * tt2), sign(sin(3 * tt2))) # two sources X <- S %*% matrix(c(1, 1, -1, 2), 2) # two mixed "microphones" ica <- fastICA::fastICA(X, n.comp = 2) par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1)) matplot(S, type = "l", lty = 1, main = "sources"); matplot(X, type = "l", lty = 1, main = "mixtures") matplot(ica$S, type = "l", lty = 1, main = "ICA estimates") ``` ::: ## Summary ::: instructions - Functional data: smooth curves observed discretely with noise; think of each curve as **one** observation. - Represent with basis expansions (Fourier for periodic, B-splines in general); control roughness with a penalty and choose $\lambda$ by GCV. - Surfaces: tensor-product bases; irregular domains: triangulations. - Variation: SVD/PCA $\rightarrow$ functional PCA (eigenfunctions and scores); regularize for noisy or incomplete curves. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
